title: Your first Dune project: a library and an executable
body: Dune is the standard build system for OCaml. A project is a directory with a `dune-project` file naming the Dune language version, and one or more `dune` files that declare what to build. `dune build` compiles everything, `dune exec bin/main.exe` runs a program, and `dune clean` removes the `_build` directory.

Split code into a library and an executable. A `(library (name greeter))` stanza turns every module in its directory into part of the library `Greeter`, and an `(executable (name main) (libraries greeter))` stanza links against it. Dune works out the dependency order itself, so you never list source files by hand.

Everything Dune generates lives in `_build`, which you do not edit or commit. When a build fails, read the first error: Dune prints the file, line and the compiler message, and re-running `dune build` only recompiles what changed.
challenge: Open src/greeter.ml and make `greet name` return "Hello, <name>!". Then run `dune exec --root . bin/main.exe` and confirm it prints the greeting for "world".
projectInstructions: Work inside the project directory. Run `dune build --root .` to compile and `dune exec --root . bin/main.exe` to run. Change only src/greeter.ml.
question: What does the `(libraries greeter)` field in an executable's dune file do?
correct: It links the executable against the library named greeter defined elsewhere in the project
wrong: It installs a package called greeter from opam
It copies greeter.ml into the executable's directory
reasoning: A library stanza defines a named unit of code; listing it in libraries lets another stanza use its modules.
